lessons.title: Preconception folic acid
lessons.objective: Prescribe preconception folic acid with the right dose, start and duration, recognise who needs a high-dose plan and separate NTD prevention from fertility promises.
lessons.closing: Folic acid prevents NTDs: standard dose for almost everyone, an individual plan for high risk, and no “extra” dose for fertility or recurrent miscarriage.

lessons.title: MTHFR and methylfolate: what the sources say
lessons.objective: Explain why a common MTHFR variant does not contraindicate folic acid and why routine genotyping or homocysteine testing is not recommended.
lessons.closing: The common variant does not change the recommendation: standard folic acid, no extra tests, and a reassuring explanation.

lessons.title: Vitamin D: pregnancy, fertility and losses
lessons.objective: Distinguish empiric supplementation in pregnancy, correction of a deficiency with an indication and fertility claims, separating association from efficacy and clinical pregnancy from live birth.
lessons.closing: Vitamin D: reasonable in pregnancy with low certainty, without routine screening, and without trial evidence that it improves IVF outcomes or recurrent loss.

items.title: Preconception folic acid: who, how much and when
items.core: USPSTF recommends (grade A) that everyone who plans to or could become pregnant take a daily supplement containing 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) of folic acid, from at least 1 month before conception through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]]
items.body:
Indication: prevention of neural tube defects (NTDs), not fertility enhancement. USPSTF judges with high certainty that the net benefit is substantial and that, at usual doses, folic acid is not associated with serious harms. It insists on the supplement even where foods are fortified, because dietary intake is often insufficient. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]]

NICE agrees in substance with a slightly different schedule: 400 micrograms a day, ideally from 3 months before trying to conceive (or as soon as pregnancy is known) and for at least the first 12 weeks, even with fortified flour. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]
items.recall: What dose, from when and until when does USPSTF recommend folic acid?

rows.text: Plans to or could become pregnant

visual.alt: Diagram: for anyone planning or able to become pregnant, daily folic acid 400–800 µg per USPSTF or 400 µg per NICE, from at least 1 month before (ideally 3 months per NICE) until the first 2–3 months or 12 weeks of pregnancy.

items.application: Ask about folic acid at any visit with a woman who could become pregnant, not only when she says she is trying: many pregnancies are unplanned.
items.pearl: Preconception folic acid = NTD prevention. If someone sells it as “to get pregnant”, the outcome is the wrong one.

items.title: High NTD risk: an individual plan, not the standard dose
items.core: The USPSTF recommendation does not apply to people with a previous NTD-affected pregnancy or other very-high-risk situations; they may need higher doses and should discuss it with their clinician. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]]
items.body:
NICE is specific: offer 5 mg a day of folic acid, when planning and in the first 12 weeks, when there is an increased risk of NTD or other congenital malformation. Examples it gives: NTD or malformation in the person, their partner or family; a previous affected pregnancy; type 1 or 2 diabetes; a haematological condition requiring folic acid (sickle cell disease, thalassaemia); or medicines that affect folate absorption or metabolism, such as anti-epileptics or HIV medicines. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]

After bariatric surgery, NICE refers to the bariatric unit for individual advice on folic acid and other micronutrients. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]
items.recall: Which situations, per NICE, justify high-dose folic acid?
items.application: Before “giving the usual folic acid”, review NTD history, diabetes, haemoglobinopathies, bariatric surgery and medicines (especially anti-epileptics). If any is present, the dose belongs to an individual plan with local guidance and the relevant specialist (neurology, endocrinology, haematology).
items.pearl: Mind the units: 400 µg is 0.4 mg; 5 mg is more than ten times that dose. Mixing up µg and mg on a prescription is a classic error.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG247 (2025); USPSTF 2023 excludes high risk.

items.title: Myth: “more folic acid, more fertility and fewer miscarriages”
items.core: In unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent further losses; ESHRE advises against high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions that raise NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
Strong ESHRE recommendation: low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL. In its justification, ESHRE adds that high doses should not be used without hyperhomocysteinaemia or NTD-risk conditions. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

NICE adds two common clinic situations in which there is no need to go above 400 µg a day, unless another risk factor from its list is present: BMI ≥25 kg/m² and increased risk of pre-eclampsia. [[ref:nice-2025-ng247]]
items.recall: Does folic acid prevent unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss?
items.application: If a patient with recurrent miscarriage asks for “the high dose” so as not to lose again, you can explain that the standard dose is still for NTD prevention and that increasing it does not protect against miscarriage.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE RPL 2022: strong (high dose without indication); NICE NG247.

items.stem: A healthy 29-year-old woman with no NTD history or medicines wants to try to conceive in a few months. Per USPSTF 2023, which is correct?

options.text: Folic acid 0.4–0.8 mg daily from at least 1 month before conception through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: this is the USPSTF grade A recommendation.

options.text: Start folic acid once pregnancy is confirmed, since before that it adds no benefit.
options.why: The neural tube closes very early; that is why it should start at least 1 month before conception.

options.text: Folic acid 5 mg daily, because more dose means more protection.
options.why: High doses are reserved for increased-risk situations; this woman has none.

options.text: No supplement is needed if her diet includes fortified foods.
options.why: USPSTF and NICE recommend the supplement even with fortification.

items.explanation: Standard dose, starting before conception and continuing into the first trimester: that is how the neural-tube closure window is protected.

items.stem: Per NICE NG247, which of these women planning pregnancy has an indication for high-dose folic acid (5 mg/day)?

options.text: 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes.
options.why: Correct: type 1 or 2 diabetes is among NICE’s increased-risk factors.

options.text: 34-year-old woman with BMI 31 kg/m² and no other factors.
options.why: NICE states that BMI ≥25 does not require more than 400 µg unless another risk factor is present.

options.text: 30-year-old woman at increased risk of pre-eclampsia and no other factors.
options.why: NICE explicitly reassures: pre-eclampsia risk does not require going above 400 µg.

options.text: 33-year-old woman heterozygous for MTHFR C677T.
options.why: Carrying a common MTHFR variant is not listed as an indication; carriers process folic acid.

items.explanation: High doses respond to specific factors (NTD history, diabetes, haemoglobinopathies, folate-altering medicines), not to weight or a common genotype.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with three early miscarriages, unremarkable RPL work-up, no diabetes or epilepsy. She asks for high-dose folic acid “so I don’t lose it again”. Per ESHRE, what is appropriate?

options.text: Keep the low preconception dose to prevent NTDs and explain that it does not prevent loss; do not use a high dose.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE (strong): low-dose folic acid does not prevent loss; according to its justification, high doses should not be used without an indication.

options.text: Prescribe 5 mg daily: RPL is an NTD risk factor.
options.why: Unexplained RPL is not among the factors justifying a high dose.

options.text: Stop folic acid because it has no effect on RPL.
options.why: It does not prevent loss, but it is still indicated to prevent NTDs.

options.text: Switch to high-dose methylfolate, which does prevent loss.
options.why: There is no verified evidence supporting that claim.

items.explanation: Separate the outcomes: folic acid prevents NTDs; it has not been shown to prevent recurrent pregnancy loss.

items.title: Myth: “with MTHFR you can’t use folic acid”
items.core: People with an MTHFR variant can process all types of folate, including folic acid, and folic acid is the only type of folate shown to help prevent NTDs. [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]]
items.body:
According to CDC, common variants are not a reason to avoid folic acid, and in the US more people have one or two copies of C677T than don't. [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]] ACOG cites C677T homozygosity of 10–16% in European populations. [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]

What remains open is how much these variants slow folate metabolism: USPSTF lists it as a research need, not as a reason to change the recommendation. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]] That 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (methylfolate) is “better” in carriers is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated result for NTD prevention.
items.recall: Can an MTHFR C677T carrier use folic acid to prevent NTDs?
items.application: If a patient brings an MTHFR report and has stopped folic acid out of fear, the priority is that she resumes NTD prevention.
items.pearl: A variant carried by most of the US population cannot, on its own, be a “disease” that contraindicates folic acid.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: CDC (public health); ACOG PB 197; USPSTF 2023 leaves it as a research area.

items.title: What I would not order: routine MTHFR genotype or homocysteine
items.core: ACOG does not recommend screening with MTHFR mutation analyses or fasting homocysteine, because of the lack of association between C677T variants and adverse pregnancy outcomes, including venous thromboembolism (Level B). [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]
items.body:
ACOG adds that MTHFR mutations by themselves do not appear to increase VTE risk, either outside or during pregnancy, and that evidence is insufficient to include them in thrombophilia work-up. [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]

For folic acid, the result would not change management either: the preconception recommendation is the same with or without a common variant. [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]]
items.recall: Why does ACOG not recommend screening MTHFR or homocysteine in pregnancy?

rows.text: Thrombophilia or pregnancy-loss work-up: not recommended (ACOG)
Choosing the folate type: does not change management (CDC)

visual.alt: Diagram: ordering MTHFR or homocysteine is not recommended to investigate thrombophilia or losses (ACOG) and does not change folate choice (CDC).

items.application: A “positive” MTHFR result can bring anxiety, expensive supplements and sometimes anticoagulation without indication. Not ordering it is also care.

items.title: Patient phrase: “my test says MTHFR”
items.core: Core message, backed by CDC: the variant is very common, your body processes folic acid and folic acid is the one shown to prevent NTDs. [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]]
items.body:
One way to put it: “Having this variant is very common: in the United States, for example, more people have it than don’t. It doesn’t mean you can’t use folic acid: you process it well, and it’s the form shown to prevent neural tube defects in the baby.” [[ref:cdc-mthfr-folic-acid]]

If she also asks about clots or miscarriage: “On its own, this variant hasn’t been linked to more clots or worse pregnancy outcomes, so guidelines don’t use it to decide treatments.” [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]
items.recall: How would you explain to a patient that her MTHFR variant does not contraindicate folic acid?
items.application: Validate the concern before correcting the fact, and write down what to take and at what dose.

items.stem: A 30-year-old patient trying to conceive brings an “MTHFR C677T heterozygous” genotype from a commercial lab and has stopped folic acid because she read she “can’t metabolise it”. Which answer fits the sources?

options.text: Resume folic acid at the standard dose: carriers process folic acid and it is the form with proven efficacy against NTDs.
options.why: Correct: this is CDC’s position; the common variant is not a reason to avoid it.

options.text: Replace it with methylfolate, which has been shown to prevent NTDs better in carriers.
options.why: CDC states folic acid is the only folate type shown to prevent NTDs; methylfolate superiority is a hypothesis.

options.text: Order fasting homocysteine before deciding.
options.why: ACOG does not recommend fasting homocysteine screening in pregnancy, and it would not change the folic acid recommendation.

options.text: Prescribe 5 mg folic acid to compensate for the variant.
options.why: A common variant is not among NICE’s high-dose indications.

items.explanation: The common variant does not change the recommendation: standard-dose folic acid, with no extra tests.

items.stem: When reviewing a thrombophilia panel for a pregnant woman, which test does ACOG not recommend?

options.text: MTHFR genotype and fasting homocysteine.
options.why: Correct: ACOG does not recommend this screening due to the lack of association with adverse outcomes (Level B).

options.text: None: the more tests, the better the stratification.
options.why: More tests without clinical utility create false “positives”, anxiety and unindicated treatment.

options.text: MTHFR yes, because C677T homozygosity clearly increases VTE risk.
options.why: ACOG states MTHFR mutations by themselves do not appear to increase VTE risk.

items.explanation: MTHFR and homocysteine add nothing to thrombophilia evaluation in pregnancy according to ACOG.

items.title: Vitamin D: empiric in pregnancy, no routine 25(OH)D
items.core: The Endocrine Society suggests empiric vitamin D during pregnancy (conditional, low certainty) and suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing in healthy pregnant individuals without an established indication (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:endo-2024-vitamin-d]]
items.body:
Indication: possible reduction of pre-eclampsia, intrauterine mortality, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth and neonatal mortality. Trials used 600 to 5000 IU (15–125 µg) daily equivalent; the guideline acknowledges the optimal dose is unclear and asks to stay within the IOM tolerable upper intake level. [[ref:endo-2024-vitamin-d]]

Before pregnancy, in healthy adults under 50, the same guideline suggests no supplementation above the recommended intake (600 IU [15 µg] a day) and no routine 25(OH)D testing, noting that 25(OH)D thresholds with outcome benefit have not been established in trials. None of this applies to people with an established indication, such as hypocalcaemia. [[ref:endo-2024-vitamin-d]]
items.recall: What does the Endocrine Society 2024 suggest about supplementing and testing vitamin D in pregnancy?
items.application: Correcting a deficiency documented for a clinical indication is different from empiric supplementation: make clear in the record which of the two you are doing and why.
items.pearl: 1 µg of vitamin D = 40 IU: 15 µg = 600 IU. Always check which unit the label uses.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Endocrine Society 2024: conditional; low (supplement) and very low (no testing) certainty.

items.title: Discrepancy: conditional guideline versus Cochrane “very uncertain”
items.core: The 2024 Cochrane review, after removing 20 studies over trustworthiness concerns, concludes that the effect of vitamin D alone on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth is very uncertain. [[ref:cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy]]
items.body:
In the vitamin D versus placebo or nothing comparison (8 studies, 2313 pregnant women), it may reduce severe postpartum haemorrhage (a single study, low certainty) and low birthweight, although the interval does not rule out an increase. The authors call for large, rigorous trials, including on maternal adverse effects. [[ref:cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy]]

The Endocrine Society suggests supplementation with low certainty. [[ref:endo-2024-vitamin-d]] This is not a head-on contradiction: a conditional recommendation with low certainty and a review finding very uncertain effects describe the same gap in high-quality evidence.
items.recall: What changed in the 2024 Cochrane review on vitamin D in pregnancy, and what does it conclude?

rows.text: Endocrine Society 2024: suggests empiric (conditional, low certainty)
Cochrane 2024: very uncertain effects on pre-eclampsia, GDM and preterm birth

visual.alt: Comparison: the Endocrine Society 2024 suggests empiric vitamin D in pregnancy with low certainty; Cochrane 2024 finds very uncertain effects on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth.

items.pearl: When a review removes studies for trustworthiness, earlier “moderate” estimates can disappear. Check the version and date of the review you cite.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: Cochrane 2024: low to very low certainty.

items.title: Vitamin D and IVF: association is not efficacy
items.core: In assisted-reproduction cohorts, vitamin D-replete women had more live births (OR 1.33; 95% CI 1.08–1.65), but this is an observational association and the authors call for a trial to test whether correcting deficiency helps. [[ref:chu-2018-vitd-art]]
items.body:
The SUNDRO RCT tested it in 630 women with 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL, normal weight and preserved reserve: a single 600,000 IU dose of vitamin D3 before IVF did not improve clinical pregnancy (37% vs 40%; RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.75–1.11), and no exploratory subgroup benefited. [[ref:somigliana-2021-sundro]]

A 2023 meta-analysis mixing 9 RCTs and 3 cohorts reports more clinical pregnancy (OR 1.70), with high heterogeneity, six studies using multicomponent products (e.g. with inositol or melatonin) and no pooling of live births; with vitamin D alone the effect was not significant unless SUNDRO was excluded. [[ref:meng-2023-vitd-infertility]]
items.recall: What did the SUNDRO RCT show about vitamin D before IVF?

rows.text: Cohorts: replete vitamin D ↔ more live births
SUNDRO RCT: no improvement in clinical pregnancy
Mixed meta-analysis: clinical pregnancy, live birth not pooled

visual.alt: Diagram: in cohorts, replete vitamin D is associated with more live births; the SUNDRO RCT showed no improvement in clinical pregnancy with supplementation; a mixed meta-analysis reports clinical pregnancy without pooling live births.

items.application: If a woman going to IVF is supplemented, let it be for general reasons (pregnancy, deficiency with an indication), not with a promise of more pregnancies.
items.pearl: Always ask: association or trial? Clinical pregnancy or live birth? Vitamin D alone or a “cocktail”?

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: Cohorts (association); one negative RCT; mixed meta-analysis of limited quality.

items.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss: vitamin D may be considered, testing it not
items.core: ESHRE proposes that preconception counselling in RPL may include considering prophylactic vitamin D (good practice), although evidence of effectiveness is absent, and does not recommend testing vitamin D to find a cause or guide treatment. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body: The reasoning: deficiency seems common in women with RPL (47.4% below 30 ng/mL in a case-control study) and is associated with obstetric complications, but there is no indication that vitamin D status contributes to RPL, nor studies measuring its effect on live birth in the next pregnancy. The guideline considers supplementation safe. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE say about testing and supplementing vitamin D in RPL?
items.application: You can offer it as a general pregnancy-health measure, explaining that it is not a treatment for recurrent loss.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE RPL 2022: good practice point (GPP), no evidence of effectiveness.

items.stem: A healthy pregnant woman at 10 weeks, no hypocalcaemia or other indication. Per the Endocrine Society 2024, what is appropriate regarding vitamin D?

options.text: Consider an empiric supplement without routine 25(OH)D testing.
options.why: Correct: it suggests empiric vitamin D and against routine 25(OH)D testing (both conditional).

options.text: Measure 25(OH)D and supplement only if <30 ng/mL.
options.why: The guideline suggests against routine testing and notes no trial-established benefit thresholds.

options.text: Measure 25(OH)D every trimester to adjust the dose.
options.why: There is no recommendation for serial monitoring in healthy pregnant women.

options.text: Do not supplement, because evidence shows it has no effect.
options.why: The evidence is uncertain, not negative; the guideline suggests supplementation with low certainty.

items.explanation: Conditional suggestion: supplement without 25(OH)D screening, unless there is an established clinical indication.

items.stem: In the SUNDRO RCT (women with 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL before IVF), what result was obtained with a single high dose of vitamin D3 versus placebo?

options.text: It did not improve the clinical pregnancy rate (37% vs 40%).
options.why: Correct: RR 0.91 (95% CI 0.75–1.11), with no benefiting subgroups.

options.text: It significantly increased live births.
options.why: The primary outcome was clinical pregnancy and it did not improve; an increase in live births cannot be claimed.

options.text: It improved only in women with more severe deficiency.
options.why: Exploratory analyses by baseline 25(OH)D did not identify benefit.

options.text: It reduced miscarriages, though clinical pregnancy did not change.
options.why: Miscarriage was a secondary outcome; the trial does not show that vitamin D reduces it, and an effect on miscarriage cannot be claimed without an effect on clinical pregnancy.

items.explanation: The observational association was not confirmed in the trial: correcting vitamin D before IVF did not increase clinical pregnancy.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the evidence on vitamin D and assisted-reproduction outcomes in women?

options.text: Cohorts show an association between replete vitamin D and live birth, but the largest RCT showed no benefit of supplementation on clinical pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: it separates association (Chu 2018) from trial efficacy (SUNDRO 2021).

options.text: RCTs show that supplementation increases live birth.
options.why: The 2023 meta-analysis did not pool live births and SUNDRO did not improve clinical pregnancy.

options.text: Low vitamin D causes infertility, as cohorts demonstrate.
options.why: Cohorts show association, not causation; confounding is possible.

options.text: The 2023 meta-analysis proves the efficacy of vitamin D alone on live birth.
options.why: It mixes designs and multicomponent products; with vitamin D alone the effect was not significant unless SUNDRO was excluded, and live births were not pooled.

items.explanation: Association, clinical pregnancy and live birth are different rungs; for vitamin D in IVF the trial rung has not been cleared.

acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 197: Inherited Thrombophilias in Pregnancy
acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.authors: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists' Committee on Practice Bulletins—Obstetrics
acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.population: Pregnant women and women considered for inherited thrombophilia evaluation.
acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.finding: Because of the lack of association between heterozygosity or homozygosity for MTHFR C677T and adverse pregnancy outcomes (including VTE), screening with MTHFR mutation analyses or fasting homocysteine is not recommended (Level B). MTHFR mutations by themselves do not appear to increase VTE risk.
acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia.limitations: Full text read (Obstet Gynecol 2018;132:e18–34) from an academic copy of the published PDF. Whether ACOG has reaffirmed or replaced it after 2018 was not verified. US context.

cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.title: MTHFR Gene Variant and Folic Acid Facts
cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.population: People who can become pregnant, including carriers of MTHFR variants (US).
cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.finding: People with MTHFR variants can process all types of folate, including folic acid; folic acid is the only type of folate shown to help prevent neural tube defects; common variants are not a reason to avoid it. The C677T variant is very common in the US.
cdc-mthfr-folic-acid.limitations: Public-health information page (not a GRADE guideline); read in full. Date shown on the page: 16 July 2026 (not stated whether publication or review).

chu-2018-vitd-art.title: Vitamin D and assisted reproductive treatment outcome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
chu-2018-vitd-art.authors: Chu J, Gallos I, Tobias A, Tan B, Eapen A, Coomarasamy A
chu-2018-vitd-art.population: 11 cohort studies (2700 women) undergoing assisted reproduction.
chu-2018-vitd-art.finding: Vitamin D-replete women had more live births than deficient/insufficient women (OR 1.33; 95% CI 1.08–1.65; 7 studies, 2026 women); no association with miscarriage. The authors call for an RCT to test whether correcting deficiency helps.
chu-2018-vitd-art.limitations: Structured abstract read. Observational data (association, possible confounding); heterogeneous populations and protocols.

cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.title: Vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy
cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.authors: Palacios C, Kostiuk LL, Cuthbert A, Weeks J
cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.population: Pregnant women in randomised trials of vitamin D alone or combined (10 studies included after trustworthiness assessment).
cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.finding: After removing 20 studies over trustworthiness concerns, the effect of vitamin D alone on pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth is very uncertain; it may reduce severe postpartum haemorrhage (1 study) and low birthweight (an increase not ruled out).
cochrane-2024-vitd-pregnancy.limitations: Full abstract read; GRADE tables of the full text not read. Assesses pregnancy, not fertility.

endo-2024-vitamin-d.title: Vitamin D for the Prevention of Disease: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
endo-2024-vitamin-d.authors: Demay MB, Pittas AG, Bikle DD, Diab DL, Kiely ME, Lazaretti-Castro M, Lips P, Mitchell DM, Murad MH, Powers S, Rao SD, Scragg R, Tayek JA, Valent AM, Walsh JME, McCartney CR
endo-2024-vitamin-d.population: Generally healthy population without established indications for vitamin D treatment or testing, including pregnant individuals.
endo-2024-vitamin-d.finding: Pregnancy: suggests empiric vitamin D (conditional, low certainty; trials used 600–5000 IU [15–125 µg] daily equivalent; optimal dose unclear) and suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing (conditional, very low). Adults <50: no supplementation above the recommended intake (600 IU [15 µg]) and no routine 25(OH)D testing (conditional, very low).
endo-2024-vitamin-d.limitations: Abstract, recommendation list and technical remarks read on the journal website; the full justification of the pregnancy section was not read. Does not address fertility or IVF. Does not apply to people with established indications (e.g. hypocalcaemia).

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment.
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based.

meng-2023-vitd-infertility.title: Influence of Vitamin D supplementation on reproductive outcomes of infertile patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
meng-2023-vitd-infertility.authors: Meng X, Zhang J, Wan Q, Huang J, Han T, Qu T, Yu LL
meng-2023-vitd-infertility.population: 12 studies (9 RCTs and 3 cohorts; 2352 infertile women); 6 used multicomponent products containing vitamin D.
meng-2023-vitd-infertility.finding: Higher clinical pregnancy rate with vitamin D (OR 1.70; 95% CI 1.24–2.34; I² 63%), no differences in implantation, biochemical pregnancy or miscarriage. With vitamin D alone the effect was not significant unless the SUNDRO trial was excluded. Live birth was not pooled.
meng-2023-vitd-infertility.limitations: Full text read (Europe PMC). Mixes RCTs and cohorts, high heterogeneity, co-interventions (inositol, melatonin, etc.) and highly variable regimens; no GRADE assessment.

nice-2025-ng247.title: Maternal and child nutrition: nutrition and weight management in pregnancy, and nutrition in children up to 5 years (NG247)
nice-2025-ng247.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2025-ng247.population: People planning a pregnancy or who are pregnant, and children up to 5 years (UK).
nice-2025-ng247.finding: 400 micrograms/day of folic acid from before trying to conceive (ideally 3 months) and for at least the first 12 weeks, even with fortification; 5 mg/day for increased risk of neural tube defect (personal/family history or previous affected pregnancy, type 1 or 2 diabetes, haematological conditions requiring it, medicines affecting folate such as anti-epileptics or HIV medicines); BMI ≥25 or pre-eclampsia risk do not need more than 400 µg. Avoid supplements containing vitamin A (retinol) or cod liver oil in pregnancy.
nice-2025-ng247.limitations: Recommendations 1.1.x (folic acid and vitamins section) read on the NICE website; evidence reviews not read. UK context.

somigliana-2021-sundro.title: Single oral dose of vitamin D3 supplementation prior to in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer in normal weight women: the SUNDRO randomized controlled trial
somigliana-2021-sundro.authors: Somigliana E, Sarais V, Reschini M, Ferrari S, Makieva S, Cermisoni GC, Paffoni A, Papaleo E, Vigano P
somigliana-2021-sundro.population: 630 women aged 18–39 with 25(OH)D <30 ng/mL, BMI 18–25 and AMH >0.5 ng/mL, in their 1st–3rd IVF/ICSI cycle (Italy).
somigliana-2021-sundro.finding: A single oral dose of 600,000 IU of vitamin D3 versus placebo did not improve cumulative clinical pregnancy (37% vs 40%; RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.75–1.11); no exploratory subgroup benefited.
somigliana-2021-sundro.limitations: Structured abstract read. Primary outcome: clinical pregnancy (live birth secondary, not verified here). Single high-dose regimen; normal-weight women with preserved reserve.

uspstf-2023-folic-acid.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: US Preventive Services Task Force Reaffirmation Recommendation Statement
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.population: People who plan to or could become pregnant (US); does not apply to those with a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or other very-high-risk situations.
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.finding: Grade A: daily supplement containing 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) of folic acid, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. No serious harms at usual doses; MTHFR variants are listed as a research need.
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.limitations: Statement read on the USPSTF website (full recommendation text); the JAMA evidence review was not read. US context with flour fortification; gives no dose for high risk.
